lesson.title: Naming the Line: The Linearization Formula
lesson.summary: The tangent line approximation has a formula, L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a), which packages the starting height, the slope, and the distance traveled into one reusable function.
lesson.body:
The tangent line approximation from the previous chapter deserves its own name and its own formula. The linearization of f at a is L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a). Each piece has a job: f(a) is where you start, the known height of the curve at the point of tangency; f'(a) is the slope, telling you how fast the curve was rising or falling right at that point; and (x - a) is how far you have stepped away from a. Multiply the slope by the distance traveled and add it to the starting height, and you get an estimate of where the curve now sits.

Nothing here is new mathematics: L(x) is just the tangent line written in point-slope form, the same line described geometrically before. What is new is treating it as a function you build once and can plug any nearby x into, rather than a one-time geometric picture. That reusability is what makes linearization a working tool instead of just an observation.

Try it on a cube. Let f(x) = x^3 and a = 2. Then f(2) = 8, and since f'(x) = 3x^2, f'(2) = 3(4) = 12. The linearization is L(x) = 8 + 12(x - 2). Use it to estimate 2.05^3 without multiplying 2.05 by itself twice: L(2.05) = 8 + 12(0.05) = 8 + 0.6 = 8.6. Multiplying it out directly gives 2.05^3 = 2.05 * 2.05 * 2.05 = 4.2025 * 2.05 = 8.615125, so the linearization is off by about 0.015, roughly 0.2 percent of the true value, a small price for skipping the exact arithmetic.

The formula works in either direction: x can sit above a or below it, and the same L(x) handles both. Once f(a) and f'(a) are known at a single convenient point, L(x) becomes a cheap substitute for f(x) at any x close enough to that point.
